standard.title: Assertive consent communication
standard.description: explain and apply skills and strategies to communicate assertively and respectfully when seeking, giving or denying consent
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have described strategies for seeking, giving or denying consent and rehearsed how to communicate their intentions effectively and respectfully (Y5-6). They have practised communication strategies in basic scenarios but have not yet been expected to explain the rationale behind assertive communication or apply it across more complex relationship and digital contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain and apply skills and strategies to communicate assertively and respectfully when seeking, giving or denying consent.

nodes.label: Understanding consent and assertive communication
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what consent means in different relationship types and describe what assertive, respectful communication looks like compared to passive or aggressive communication.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what consent means in at least one relationship context and describe one characteristic of assertive (as distinct from aggressive or passive) communication.
nodes.typical_width: Explain consent across different relationship types (friendships, romantic/sexual relationships, online interactions); describe the characteristics of assertive communication; explain why assertiveness protects both parties in a consent interaction.
wider: Examine the nature of consent in different types of relationships — including online and digital contexts — and identify what makes consent communication more complex in each
Investigate how online and social protocols differ from face-to-face consent communication, and what strategies protect wellbeing in online interactions
nodes.hinge_reason: Application of assertive consent communication requires students to know what they are trying to achieve — students who cannot distinguish assertive from passive or aggressive communication will not be able to recognise or practise the specific communication skills the descriptor requires.

response_modes.reason: Use clear conceptual differentiation: assertive (clear, respectful, self-respecting), passive (unclear, deferring), aggressive (disrespectful, coercive). Apply the distinction to consent scenarios before practising the skill.

success_criteria: Explains what consent means in at least one relationship context
Describes at least one characteristic of assertive communication that distinguishes it from passive or aggressive communication

nodes.label: Exploring skills and strategies for consent communication
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain specific skills and strategies for seeking, giving and denying consent assertively and respectfully, including in online contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one skill or strategy for communicating assertively when seeking, giving or denying consent and explain why it is effective.
nodes.typical_width: Explore and refine a range of skills and strategies for assertive consent communication across in-person and online contexts; recognise and respond to harmful online content (grooming, image-based abuse); explain how digital communication creates additional challenges for consent.
wider: Explore strategies for recognising and responding to online content that may be harmful — such as grooming or image-based abuse — and practise communicating needs or concerns assertively in these situations
Examine how power imbalances, group pressure and digital contexts complicate consent communication, and identify strategies that remain effective in these more challenging conditions

response_modes.reason: Students need multiple strategies across multiple contexts — no single strategy works in all consent situations. Building a repertoire that spans in-person and online contexts is essential before application.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Online and digital consent contexts represent genuinely new terrain where students lack established scripts — investing width here builds strategies that are practically relevant to the situations young people most frequently encounter.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one skill or strategy for assertive consent communication
Explains why the skill or strategy is effective for seeking, giving or denying consent

nodes.label: Applying consent communication skills
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply skills and strategies for assertive, respectful consent communication in a range of scenarios, demonstrating the ability to seek, give and deny consent.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least one assertive consent communication strategy in a practice scenario involving seeking, giving or denying consent.
nodes.typical_width: Apply consent communication skills across multiple scenarios including face-to-face and online/digital contexts; practise seeking, giving and denying consent assertively; evaluate the effectiveness of strategies used in each scenario.
wider: Examine and practise strategies for assertive consent communication in situations where consent is complicated by power imbalances or digital dynamics

Design and role-play scenarios that require assertive consent communication in a range of realistic relationship and digital contexts, reflecting on what made each scenario challenging and what strategies were most effective

response_modes.reason: Assertive communication is a practiced skill — role-play and scenario practice need to be repeated across varied scenarios to build the confidence and habit that enables real-world application.

success_criteria: Applies at least one assertive consent communication strategy in a practice scenario
Demonstrates the ability to seek, give or deny consent in the scenario
Evaluates the effectiveness of the strategy used
